outline.description: Sets the stage with the facts leading to the felon-in-possession charge, the evidence recovered, the trial results, and the sentencing context that frame the appellate issues.
subtopics: Incident overview (Nov. 19–20, 2020): Cutbank’s drug/alcohol use; pointing a gun at D.F.; forcing her into a closet; threats; striking her; rousing others in the home; flight with phone and gun
Police response at nearby garage: barricade; erratic statements; claim of weapon; resistance; biting an officer; grabbing an officer’s gun
Recovered evidence along route: D.F.’s phone; butcher knife; sawed-off Marlin .22 rifle; DNA match to Cutbank
Witness identification: D.F. and C.F. recognized the same sawed-off rifle from prior occasions
Trial results: jury conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1); jury finding of at least three prior violent felonies triggering § 924(e) (ACCA) penalties
Sentencing: advisory Guidelines calculations; 292-month within-range sentence; issues preserved for appeal
Issues on appeal: multiple evidentiary/procedural rulings alleged to have denied a fair trial; challenge to USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) four-level enhancement and to the sentence’s reasonableness

outline.chapter_title: Evidentiary Framework and Standards of Review
outline.description: Explains the governing evidentiary doctrines and appellate standards necessary to understand how the Eighth Circuit evaluated each challenged ruling.
subtopics: Standard of review: abuse of discretion for evidentiary rulings and decisions on limiting instructions
Intrinsic evidence vs. Rule 404(b) propensity evidence: prior possession of the same firearm as proof of later possession (United States v. Battle)
Hearsay and Confrontation Clause: no violation when declarant testifies at trial (United States v. Charboneau)
Limiting instructions: court need not instruct contemporaneously if an appropriate final instruction is given (United States v. Bennett)
Rule 403 balancing: excluding evidence only if probative value is substantially outweighed by unfair prejudice or confusion
Impeachment by prior inconsistent statements: extrinsic evidence must be properly authenticated (United States v. Cumbie)
Harmless error: reversal only if the verdict may have been substantially swayed (United States v. DeMarce); cumulative error requires substantial prejudice (United States v. Keys)

outline.chapter_title: Applying the Law to the Five Trial Rulings (A–E)
outline.description: Walks through each evidentiary/procedural challenge, showing how the court applied the frameworks to affirm the district court’s decisions.
subtopics: A. Prior sightings of the sawed-off rifle by D.F. and C.F.: admissible as intrinsic evidence directly relevant to possession and continuous control; not barred by Rule 404(b) (Battle)
B. Denial of pretrial limiting instruction re: D.F.’s statements to police: no abuse where no hearsay was admitted, declarant testified, and Confrontation Clause was satisfied (Bennett; Charboneau)
C. Renewed objections to prior-sighting testimony at trial: overruled consistently with pretrial intrinsic-evidence ruling

D. Refusal to strike D.F.’s statement that her sister was killed by a gun: came in as explanation for inconsistent statements elicited on cross; minimal risk of unfair prejudice; permissible under Rule 403; C.F. made a similar, unobjected statement

E. Limits on reading from a police report to impeach C.F.: proper to require authentication because the report was authored by the officer, not the witness; cross-examination about what C.F. told police was allowed (Cumbie)

Harmless/cumulative error resolution: substantial physical and testimonial evidence (DNA on gun; recovery along route; witness IDs; resisting/assault on officer) meant any assumed error did not substantially influence the verdict; no cumulative prejudice

outline.description: Lays out the guideline mechanics and legal standards governing the four-level enhancement and interaction with the Armed Career Criminal Act.
subtopics: ACCA predicate finding by jury under 18 U.S.C. § 924(e) and application of the Armed Career Criminal Guideline (USSG § 4B1.4)

Guideline calculations from the PSR: base offense level 26 for sawed-off firearm under § 2K2.1(a) with two prior crimes of violence; +3 for obliterated/altered serial number; +2 for reckless endangerment during flight; +4 under § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) for possession in connection with another felony; Criminal History Category VI; advisory range 292–365 months
§ 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) and Application Note 14(C): enhancement applies if firearm was used/possessed in connection with another felony, even without a separate charge or conviction
Which offense level governs: Guidelines direct applying the greater offense level when comparing § 4B1.4 with other calculations (offense level 35 vs. ACCA level 34)

Standards of review at sentencing: correct Guidelines calculation as a procedural prerequisite (Gall; Rosales-Mireles); factual findings reviewed for clear error (United States v. Dunn); within-Guidelines sentences presumed reasonable on appeal (United States v. Goodhouse)

outline.description: Shows how the court applied the sentencing law to affirm both the enhancement and the overall sentence as procedurally and substantively reasonable.
subtopics: Enhancement application: district court adopted unobjected PSR facts establishing use/possession of the firearm in connection with another felony; no clear error under Dunn
Guideline interaction: even if ACCA guideline yielded level 34, the higher total offense level 35 properly controlled under § 4B1.4(b)
Procedural reasonableness: district court correctly calculated the range and proceeded to consider § 3553(a) (Gall; Rosales-Mireles)

Substantive reasonableness: within-Guidelines 292-month sentence presumed reasonable (Goodhouse); court reviewed submissions and factors, and need not mechanically recite them (Maluoth); presumption that arguments were considered and rejected (Masood)
Sentencing justifications: nearly a dozen prior felonies, many violent and firearm-related; domestic abuse and assaults in presence of children; injury to officer while resisting arrest
Outcome: conviction and 292-month sentence affirmed
